body:
Gujarat's place in Indian classical music

Gujarat has a rich musical heritage that includes classical music, devotional compositions and regional folk traditions. Its classical music tradition belongs predominantly to the Hindustani school of Indian classical music, which developed across northern and western India.

Classical music is distinguished by its systematic organisation around ragas and talas and by the transmission of musical knowledge through teachers, compositions and established traditions.

  • Raga: A melodic framework based on selected musical notes and their characteristic relationships.
  • Tala: An organised, recurring rhythmic cycle.
  • Gharana: A recognised musical tradition transmitted through generations of musicians and characterised by a distinctive approach to music.

Gujarat contributed to Hindustani classical music through accomplished singers, regional musical traditions, royal patronage, scholarly works and institutions of musical education.

Tana and Riri of Vadnagar

Tana and Riri were celebrated singer sisters associated with Vadnagar in present-day Mehsana district. They are remembered in Gujarati cultural tradition as pioneers of the state's classical music heritage.

The beginning of Gujarat's classical music tradition is conventionally associated with Tana-Riri of Vadnagar.

The sisters are traditionally placed in the 16th century, during the reign of the Mughal emperor Akbar. Their reputation is closely connected with the story of Tansen, one of the most celebrated musicians of Akbar's imperial court.

The legend of Tansen and Tana-Riri

According to the traditional account, Tansen performed Raga Deepak, which was believed to generate intense heat. When he subsequently suffered from a severe burning sensation, he travelled to Vadnagar in search of relief. Tana and Riri sang Raga Malhar, commonly identified in the local tradition as Megh Malhar, and relieved his suffering.

The account celebrates the sisters' mastery of classical music and the traditional association of Malhar ragas with the rainy season. The supernatural effects attributed to the ragas belong to musical folklore and should not be understood as scientifically established properties of music.

Preservation of their legacy

The Tana-Riri Memorial at Vadnagar commemorates the two sisters. The Tana-Riri Mahotsav brings together classical musicians and preserves public awareness of their contribution to Gujarat's musical heritage.

The festival, held annually at Vadnagar since 2003, is organised by the Gujarat State Sangeet Natak Akademi. Musicians are also honoured through the Tana-Riri Award.

Prelims focus

  • Tana-Riri are traditionally regarded as pioneers of Gujarat's classical music tradition.
  • They are associated with Vadnagar, Mehsana district.
  • Their traditional account belongs to the reign of Akbar.
  • Tansen is associated with Raga Deepak in the legend.
  • Tana-Riri are associated with Raga Malhar, particularly Megh Malhar.
  • Trap: Tansen was Akbar's court musician, whereas Tana-Riri are the Gujarat-associated pioneers.

[References: GCERT, Class 10 Social Science, Gujarati-medium edition, Ch. 2, Cultural Heritage of India: Traditional Handicrafts and Fine Arts, p. 12, Music; NCERT, Class 11, Living Craft Traditions of India, Theatre Crafts, p. 117; Mehsana District Administration, Places of Interest, Tanariri Memorial and Festival; Ministry of Tourism, Utsav portal, Tana Riri Mahotsav at Vadnagar 2024; GPSC, Advt. 240/2024-25, master question paper of 20 April 2025, p. 51, Q. 117, and final answer key dated 5 July 2025, Series M, Q. 117; online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

body:
Regional contributions to Hindustani music

Hindustani classical music developed through the interaction of musical traditions from different regions. Gujarat contributed distinctive melodies, compositions, musicians and theoretical works to this wider tradition.

Several raga names preserve traditional associations with the historical regions, communities or towns of Gujarat. These names are important examples of Gujarat's relationship with Indian classical music.

RagaTraditional regional association
Gujari TodiGujarat or the Gurjara tradition
SorathiSorath, a historical region of Saurashtra
KhambavatiKhambhat, formerly known as Cambay
BilavalTraditionally associated with Veraval in accounts of Gujarat's musical heritage
LatiThe historical Lata region of Gujarat

These traditional associations are useful for identifying Gujarat's musical contributions. However, a geographical association in a raga's name does not necessarily establish its exact historical place of origin.

The medieval tradition of musical scholarship

Indian classical music developed a substantial tradition of theoretical writing. Musicological treatises describe musical concepts, classify ragas and talas, and preserve knowledge that might otherwise remain confined to oral teaching.

Haripala Deva and Sangita Sudhakara

Haripala Deva is associated with the medieval musicological treatise Sangita Sudhakara, also written as Sangeet Sudhakar. His work represents an important historical contribution connected with Gujarat.

The text is part of the broader Sanskrit tradition of writing about music. Haripala Deva should be distinguished from other medieval musicologists who produced influential works on Indian music.

Related musicological works

WorkAuthorAssociation
Sangita SudhakaraHaripala DevaGujarat
Sangita RatnakaraSharngadevaDevagiri

Sangita Ratnakara is an influential Indian musicological work connected with both northern and southern classical music traditions. Its author was Sharngadeva, not Haripala Deva.

Classical music and devotional traditions

Gujarat's devotional traditions also contributed to the preservation of musical knowledge. Compositions of the Bhakti poet Narsinh Mehta, including devotional songs and morning hymns known as prabhatiya, became part of the state's musical culture.

The Vaishnava tradition also developed forms of temple music in Gujarat. Haveli Sangeet, associated with the Pushtimarg tradition of Krishna worship, uses devotional compositions that may be based on classical ragas.

A raga is a melodic framework, whereas a devotional song is a composition expressing religious devotion. A devotional composition can use a classical raga without becoming a separate classical music school.

Prelims focus

  • Sorathi is associated with Sorath in Saurashtra.
  • Khambavati is associated with Khambhat or Cambay.
  • Haripala Deva authored Sangita Sudhakara.
  • Sharngadeva authored Sangita Ratnakara.
  • Haveli Sangeet belongs to the Vaishnava devotional music tradition.

[References: GCERT, Class 7 Social Science, Gujarati-medium edition, Ch. 4, Medieval Architecture, Cities, Merchants and Craftsmen, Music section, and Ch. 7, Bhakti Age: Religious Sects and Saints; GCERT, Class 10 Social Science, Gujarati-medium edition, Ch. 2, p. 12, Music; Government of Gujarat, NRI Division, Dance and Music, regional ragas and temple music sections; online source consulted 25 November 2026.]
title: Regional Ragas and Historical Music Texts of Gujarat

body:
Royal patronage of classical music

Before independence, the princely states of Gujarat played an important role in supporting classical musicians. Their rulers appointed court musicians, organised performances and provided financial assistance to artists and teachers.

Such patronage enabled accomplished musicians to devote themselves to the study, composition, performance and teaching of music. It also encouraged the movement of musicians between different regions of India.

Among Gujarat's princely states, Baroda, present-day Vadodara, emerged as an important centre of Hindustani classical music under the Gaekwad dynasty.

Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III

Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III ruled Baroda from 1875 to 1939. He was an important patron of education, literature, arts and classical music.

His contribution to classical music went beyond employing musicians at the royal court. He supported institutional music education, encouraged scholarly study of music and brought leading musicians and musicologists together.

Musicians associated with the Baroda court

Baroda attracted musicians from different regions and musical traditions. Important figures associated with its musical heritage include:

  • Ustad Maula Bakhsh: Musician, educator and founder-principal of the Baroda music school.
  • Ustad Faiyaz Khan: A distinguished Hindustani vocalist belonging to the Agra gharana.
  • Ustad Abdul Karim Khan: A leading exponent of the Kirana gharana who served as a court musician in Baroda.
  • Hazrat Inayat Khan: A musician associated with Baroda's musical tradition.

These musicians did not all belong to a single gharana. Baroda's importance arose partly from its ability to bring together different musical traditions under a common system of patronage.

From court patronage to formal education

In February 1886, Sayajirao Gaekwad III established the Gayan Shala in Baroda. Ustad Maula Bakhsh, also spelled Mawla Bux or Maulabaksh, became its founder-principal.

The school was originally known as Chhokarao Ni Gayan Shala, meaning a singing school for children. Its establishment was an important step towards organised music education.

Traditional musical education largely depended on the guru-shishya parampara, in which students learned directly from a guru. The establishment of a music school supplemented this tradition with structured teaching and formal courses.

The first All-India Music Conference

In 1916, Baroda hosted the first All-India Music Conference under the patronage of Sayajirao Gaekwad III. The prominent musicologist Pandit Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande played a leading role in the conference.

The conference brought together musicians and scholars from different parts of India. It contributed to discussions about music education and the systematic study of Hindustani classical music.

Sayajirao Gaekwad III was the royal patron, Maula Bakhsh was the founder-principal of the Gayan Shala, and Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande was a leading musicologist associated with the 1916 conference.

Prelims focus

  • Baroda is the historical name of Vadodara.
  • Sayajirao Gaekwad III was a major patron of classical music.
  • Gayan Shala was established in February 1886.
  • Maula Bakhsh was its founder-principal.
  • The first All-India Music Conference was held at Baroda in 1916.
  • Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande played a leading role in the conference.

[References: The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Faculty of Performing Arts, About Faculty; Department of Indian Classical Music (Vocal), About Department, historical account of Gayan Shala and the 1916 conference; Government of Gujarat, NRI Division, Dance and Music, Baroda court musicians; Baithak Foundation, Ustad Abdul Karim Khan; online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]

body:
Life and association with Gujarat

Ustad Faiyaz Khan, also known as Faiyaz Hussain Khan, was one of the most distinguished Hindustani classical vocalists of the early 20th century.

He came from the Agra region of northern India and received his early musical training from his maternal grandfather, Ghulam Abbas Khan. He later served for many years as a court musician under Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda.

Although Faiyaz Khan did not originate from Gujarat, Vadodara became an important centre of his professional life. His association with the Baroda court made him a major figure in Gujarat's classical music heritage.

Agra gharana

Faiyaz Khan was a prominent representative of the Agra gharana, a tradition of Hindustani classical vocal music.

The Agra gharana developed from older dhrupad traditions and subsequently incorporated khayal. Faiyaz Khan became particularly renowned for his khayal singing while retaining the influence of dhrupad in his music.

Musical forms associated with Faiyaz Khan

  • Khayal: A major form of Hindustani classical vocal music that allows considerable scope for melodic elaboration within a raga.
  • Dhrupad: An older and highly structured form of Hindustani classical singing.
  • Dhamar: A traditional vocal form closely related to dhrupad.
  • Thumri: A lighter classical vocal form in which emotional expression is particularly important.

His association with several forms illustrates the breadth of his musical repertoire. Nevertheless, his principal gharana identification remains the Agra gharana.

Aftab-e-Mausiqi

Faiyaz Khan received the prestigious title Aftab-e-Mausiqi from the Maharaja of Mysore. The title means Sun of Music.

The distinction between the royal courts is important: Faiyaz Khan served as a court musician in Baroda, while the celebrated title Aftab-e-Mausiqi was conferred by the Mysore court.

He also composed musical works under the pen name Prem Piya.

Legacy in Vadodara

Faiyaz Khan contributed to the musical environment of Baroda through his performances, compositions and teaching. He died in 1950, and his tomb is located in Vadodara.

His career illustrates how a classical music tradition can spread beyond the geographical region after which its gharana is named. A musician belonging to the Agra gharana could make a lasting contribution to Gujarat while maintaining his original gharana identity.

Biographical accounts give different years for Faiyaz Khan's birth. His death in 1950, association with the Agra gharana and service at the Baroda court are consistently established facts.

Prelims focus

  • Faiyaz Khan was a Hindustani classical vocalist of the Agra gharana.
  • He was a court musician under Sayajirao Gaekwad III of Baroda.
  • Aftab-e-Mausiqi means Sun of Music.
  • The title Aftab-e-Mausiqi was conferred by the Maharaja of Mysore.
  • Prem Piya was his compositional pen name.
  • Trap: His association with Baroda does not make him a representative of the Kirana or Gwalior gharana.

[References: Sahapedia, The Agra Gharana of Hindustani Music, Faiyaz Khan section; Darbar, Ustad Faiyaz Khan, biographical profile; The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Department of Indian Classical Music (Vocal), About Department; The Times of India, Music Lovers Pay Tribute to Legendary Ustad Faiyaz Khan, 6 November 2016; online sources consulted 25 November 2026.]
